newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian rupee seen weakening late 1997-Stanchart.
newsitem.headline: Indian rupee seen weakening late 1997-Stanchart.

text.p: The Indian rupee will remain strong in the next few months but should weaken thereafter due partly to central bank intervention, according to Mitul Kotecha, treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank in London.

The rupee, trading at 35.82 to the dollar on Thursday virtually unchanged from year ago levels despite the dollar's sharp appreciation agains tother international currencies, has held its ground due to heavy foreign capital inflows into India.
"We do not expect this scenario to change; over coming months inflows are expected to remain strong yielding firm support for the rupee," Kotecha wrote in a report on the rupee.
"Further out, downward pressure on the rupee will become more apparent," he said.

He expected the rupee to come under pressure to strengthen further as inflation increased from current levels, just under six percent per annum on wholesale prices, from the effects of excessive monetary growth, an easier monetary stance and the possible implementation of a domestic petroleum price hike.
"As inflation rises there will be a further appreciation of the real exchange rate (whilst the nominal exchange rate remains stable) and a subsequent loss of competitiveness," Kotecha said.
"This loss of competitiveness will result in worsening export performance, with the authorities likely to come under fresh pressure from exporters to depreciate the rupee," he said.
He said both the Reserve bank of India and Finance Ministry had already expressed concern over the strength of the rupee.
South Asian competitors Pakistan, Sri Lanka, and Bangladesh seem to be pursuing weakening currency policies to boost competitiveness, and India may embark on a similar strategy, he said.
"Hence, we expect the rupee to succumb to gradual downward pressure due to combination of the market forces and more aggressive RBI intervention from the end of 1997," Kotecha wrote.
He did not expect political instability to have any significant effect on the rupee, which has already shown its resilience to the uncertainties of coalition politics in recent months.
